title: Investigate and Mitigate KV 'ghost' entry accumulation from concurrent eviction-write races
creator: Ava Thompson
description:
Summary: During a capacity incident on 2025-02-09 we observed sustained memory growth on several inference nodes caused by the KV cache retaining unreachable entries ("ghost entries"). These entries were not visible to normal readpaths and were only discovered via heap profiling and low-level allocator counters. Symptoms included memory pressure, OOMs on a subset of shards, and degraded tail latency for inference traffic.

Background: The KV cache uses a fixed-size slab allocator and a lock-free eviction pipeline that attempts to reclaim entries under pressure. A race between the asynchronous eviction path and concurrent write/renew operations can leave tombstoned or partially-updated entries referenced by ephemeral iterators. Under high concurrency and particular timing of compaction, these references prevent memory from being reclaimed, producing long-lived ghost entries that accumulate slowly.

What we observed:
- Rapid growth in resident set size (RSS) across several hosts over ~12 hours correlated with a spike in write-heavy requests from a single customer workload.
- Grafana alerts showed sustained "kv_slab_free_bytes" decline despite eviction rate metrics appearing nominal.
- Heap profiles and jemalloc statistics indicated live allocations backed by KV slab pages with zero visible keys in the normal index.
- Debug snapshots showed entries with zero TTL and refcounts that did not reach zero despite no active requests.

Initial hypothesis / root cause:
- A race in the eviction->compact->reclaim pipeline: when compaction moves entries and concurrently a write path performs an update using a replace/CAS, the old entry can become unreachable from the index but still reachable by an in-flight iterator/reference. Our refcounting semantics did not account for a narrow window where the iterator holds a pointer while the compaction has already unlinked the entry, preventing the usual reclamation and leaving stale pages pinned.
- Additional contributing factor: allocator rounding and slab fragmentation make those pinned pages expensive to reclaim, so the memory impact is amplified.

Immediate mitigations applied (short-term):
- Deployed a conservative eviction throttle to reduce pressure on the compaction path for high-write tenants (runtime-1.21-hotfix-3).
- Rolled out an emergency background sweep job (kv-ghost-sweeper) on a small cohort of hosts to force-check refcounts and free unreachable pages.
- Added a Grafana dashboard panel and alert (KVGhostEntries > 50 per shard sustained for 5m) and temporarily raised operator visibility.

Long-term remediation plan:
- Implement stronger pointer ownership model: convert iterator references to a safe handle that increments a stable GC epoch counter (design doc: confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/KV+Ghost+Entry+Design).
- Make compaction CAS-aware: ensure compaction sets a tombstone marker that prevents premature unlinking until safe-handles drain.
- Improve refcount accounting and add periodic sanity sweep to reconcile visible index vs allocator live pages.
- Reduce slab fragmentation by introducing slab compaction heuristics and per-tenant bucket recycling.
- Expand unit and stress tests to reproduce the race (integration harness: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/tree/main/test/kv_race_harness).

Acceptance criteria for Done:
- No ghost entry accumulation reproduction in the race harness after 12 hours of sustained load (write-heavy, high-concurrency).
- New metrics (ghost_entry_count, ghost_page_bytes, ghost_sweeper_runs) are emitting and alerts validated.
- Patch merged and rolled out to canary, with memory growth fix verified on canary for at least 48h before broad rollout.
